R: Whenever any argument of a scalar function (all functions except nps_score) is NULL, the function returns NULL.

Whenever a numeric argument (balance_cents, days_late, terms_days, avg_score, review_count, weight_grams, zone) is not a number (for example text, even digit-only text), or is NaN or infinite, the function returns NULL; fractional numbers are accepted.
Whenever a text argument of mask_card, normalize_sku, initials or invoice_check_digit is a whole integer, treat it as its decimal text; a non-integer number is NULL.
Whenever a date argument of age_years or due_date is not exactly YYYY-MM-DD (surrounding whitespace is tolerated, nothing else is) or is not a real calendar date, the function returns NULL.
Whenever late_fee gets balance_cents of zero or less, it returns 0.
Whenever late_fee gets days_late of 5 or fewer (including zero and negatives), it returns 0; there is a 5-day grace period, and 5 days late is still free.
Whenever late_fee charges a fee, it charges 2% of the balance for each started 30-day period late (days_late divided by 30, rounded up).
Whenever the late_fee percentage amount is not a whole number of cents, round it up to the next cent.
Whenever a late_fee would be below 500 cents, charge 500 cents (minimum fee), applied only when a fee is due at all.
Whenever a late_fee would be above 5000 cents, charge 5000 cents (cap).
Whenever due_date adds terms, it adds terms_days calendar days to invoice_date and returns the result as YYYY-MM-DD.
Whenever terms_days given to due_date has a fractional part, round it down to a whole number of days before applying the other term rules.
Whenever terms_days given to due_date is negative, treat it as 0.
Whenever terms_days given to due_date is above 365, treat it as 365.
Whenever the computed due date falls on a Saturday, due_date moves it forward 2 days to Monday.
Whenever the computed due date falls on a Sunday, due_date moves it forward 1 day to Monday; weekdays are never moved.
Whenever mask_card gets text, ignore every character that is not a digit (spaces, dashes, dots, letters) before masking.
Whenever mask_card finds 12 or more digits, it returns one '*' for each digit except the last four, followed by those last four digits, with no separators.
Whenever mask_card finds fewer than 12 digits, it masks every digit with '*' and shows none, returning one '*' per digit.
Whenever mask_card finds no digits (empty text or letters only), it returns an empty string, not NULL.
Whenever rating_label gets avg_score below 0 or above 5, it returns 'Invalid'; this check comes before the review-count check, so it applies even with few reviews.
Whenever rating_label gets a valid avg_score and review_count below 5 (including zero and negatives), it returns 'Unrated'; exactly 5 reviews is enough to be rated.
Whenever rating_label classifies a score, it first rounds the score to one decimal place, rounding halves up, and then applies the thresholds to the rounded value.
Whenever the rounded rating_label score is 4.5 or more, return 'Excellent'.
Whenever the rounded rating_label score is at least 3.5 and below 4.5, return 'Good'.
Whenever the rounded rating_label score is at least 2.5 and below 3.5, return 'Fair'.
Whenever the rounded rating_label score is below 2.5 (down to 0), return 'Poor'.
Whenever normalize_sku gets text, remove leading and trailing whitespace and convert letters to uppercase.
Whenever normalize_sku finds whitespace inside the text, replace each run of whitespace (any length) with a single hyphen.
Whenever normalize_sku finds a character other than A-Z, 0-9 or hyphen (punctuation, underscores, accented or other non-ASCII letters), it deletes that character, after the whitespace-to-hyphen step.
Whenever normalize_sku finds existing hyphens, keep them as they are: it never collapses repeated hyphens and never trims hyphens at the ends.
Whenever normalize_sku ends up with an empty result (empty input, or nothing but removed characters), it returns NULL.
Whenever shipping_cost gets weight_grams of zero or less, it returns 0, whatever the zone.
Whenever shipping_cost prices a positive weight, the base charge is 500 cents for zone 1, 800 for zone 2 and 1200 for zone 3.
Whenever shipping_cost gets a zone other than 1, 2 or 3 (zero, negative, above 3, or non-whole), it prices it as zone 3 and does not return NULL.
Whenever shipping_cost prices a positive weight, it adds 100 cents for each started 500 grams of weight (weight divided by 500, rounded up).
Whenever weight_grams is above 20000 (strictly), shipping_cost adds a 2500-cent oversize surcharge; exactly 20000 grams has no surcharge.
Whenever the shipping_cost total would exceed 9900 cents, it returns 9900 (cap).
Whenever initials gets a name, split it on whitespace (runs of whitespace and leading or trailing whitespace are ignored) and take the first character of each word, uppercased, in order.

Whenever a word in initials is exactly one of the all-lowercase particles van, von, de, da, di, la, del, der, den, du, le, skip it; the same word with any capital letter (for example 'Van' or 'De') counts as a normal name word.
Whenever initials meets a hyphenated or otherwise joined word, treat it as one word and use only its first character.
Whenever initials produces no letters (empty text, only whitespace, or only particles), it returns NULL.
Whenever invoice_check_digit gets text, ignore every non-digit character and work only with the digits.
Whenever invoice_check_digit finds more than 12 digits, it uses only the last 12 digits and ignores the earlier ones.
Whenever invoice_check_digit finds no digits (empty text or letters only), it returns NULL.

Whenever invoice_check_digit computes the digit, it multiplies the digits by alternating weights 3 and 1 starting with weight 3 on the rightmost digit, sums them, and returns (10 minus the sum mod 10) mod 10, so the result is 0-9.
Whenever age_years gets an as_of_date earlier than birth_date, it returns NULL; the same date gives 0.
Whenever age_years computes age, it counts completed years: the year difference, minus one if the birthday (month and day) has not yet been reached on as_of_date.
Whenever age_years gets a 29 February birth date and the as_of_date's year is not a leap year, it treats the birthday as 28 February, so the person ages on 28 February.
Whenever nps_score receives a value that is NULL, not a number, below 0 or above 10, it ignores that row entirely (it counts neither in the total nor as promoter or detractor).
Whenever nps_score classifies a valid value, 9 or more is a promoter, 6 or less is a detractor, and anything in between (including fractions such as 6.5 or 8.5) is passive.
Whenever fewer than 5 valid values reach nps_score (including an empty column), it returns NULL.

Whenever nps_score has 5 or more valid values, it returns (promoters minus detractors) divided by valid values times 100, rounded to a whole number with halves rounded away from zero (in both directions).

rules: Whenever a rule asks whether a person born on 29 February is a given age, then in years that have no 29 February the birthday counts as 28 February. For example, Meera, born 29 February 2008, is 18 on 28 February 2026, so a shop's 18+ rule says yes.

Whenever an invoice's due date is worked out, it is the issue date plus the payment terms in days. If that day is a Saturday or Sunday, the due date moves to the following Monday (for example, 1 October 2026 with 30-day terms is Saturday 31 October, so it is due Monday 2 November). Whenever an invoice is issued with payment terms of 0 days or a negative number (such as -10), accept it as is, with no rejection and no substitution of default terms. Its due date is its issue date, and the same weekend rule applies.
Whenever the system adds a check digit to a supplier's product code, ignore the letters and dash and work out the digit from the numbers only (for 'INV-2041', use 2041).

Whenever a late fee is worked out, no fee is charged unless the invoice is more than 5 days overdue. Once it is, the fee is 2% of the balance for every 30 days (or part of 30 days) the invoice is late, never less than 5.00 and never more than 50.00 (for example, Rohan's ₹10,000 invoice at 45 days would be 4%, capped at 50.00). Whenever a late fee is calculated, round it up to the next whole cent, never down or to the nearest, so any fraction of a cent above a cent boundary goes up to the next cent. A fee that is already exactly a whole cent stays as it is.

Whenever a name is turned into a badge, split it into words and skip name particles such as 'van' and 'der'. Count titles (such as 'Dr.') and suffixes (such as 'Jr.') as ordinary words, and treat a hyphenated surname as a single word that gives one initial. The badge is the first letter of each remaining word, in order. For example, 'Dr. Anna van der Berg-Smith Jr.' gives 'DABJ'.

Whenever a card number is entered for a receipt, always accept it, never refuse it and never raise an error. First remove every character that is not a digit (spaces, dashes, letters, anything else). If fewer than 12 digits remain, print one asterisk for every remaining digit (9 digits print as 9 asterisks, not a blank). If 12 or more digits remain, print every digit except the last 4 as an asterisk, followed by the last 4 digits. The result is one unbroken run with no spaces or grouping (4111 1111 1111 1234 prints ************1234).

Apply these steps in order. (1) If the average score or the review count is missing, the label is blank. (2) Otherwise, if the average is below 0 or above 5, the label is "Invalid", whatever the review count. (3) Otherwise, if there are fewer than 5 reviews, the label is "Unrated". (4) Otherwise, round the average to one decimal place with halves rounded up (4.45 counts as 4.5), then label it "Excellent" if that rounded value is 4.5 or higher, "Good" if 3.5 or higher but below 4.5, "Fair" if 2.5 or higher but below 3.5, and "Poor" if below 2.5. There is no "Very Good" label (a 4.4 average from 200 reviews is "Good").

Whenever a parcel's shipping charge is worked out, it depends only on the parcel's weight and zone, never on order value. There is no free-shipping threshold, so a 2 kg parcel costs the standard rate for 2 kg in its zone even when the basket is worth ₹2,500. Accept every weight, with no refusal and no weight limit. A parcel of 0 g or less is charged ₹0.00. For any heavier parcel, the number of blocks is the weight in grams divided by 500, rounded up. The charge is the zone's starting charge (₹9 for zone 2) + (blocks − 1) × ₹1 (2.5 kg is 5 blocks, so ₹9 + 4 × ₹1 = ₹13; 2.501 kg is 6 blocks, so ₹14). A parcel over 20 kg also gets a flat ₹25 added on top of that charge. In every zone, the total never goes above ₹99.00 (a 120 kg pallet is charged by weight as usual, then capped at ₹99.00).

Whenever the survey score is computed, count only valid answers. A valid answer is a number from 0 to 10, and this includes a 7.5, which is neither a promoter nor a detractor and is counted in the total without capping or rounding. Skip blank answers, non-numeric answers and answers outside 0 to 10 (such as 11), excluding them from the total, and never reject the survey. If there are fewer than 5 valid answers, show no score. Otherwise the score is (promoters − detractors) ÷ total valid answers × 100, rounded to a whole number. Promoters are answers of 9 or 10, detractors are answers of 0 to 6, and the total includes the 7s and 8s.

When an invoice is more than 5 days overdue but the customer's balance is ₹0 or a credit (for example ₹500 credit, 10 days past due), is a late fee charged? -> A. No late fee is charged when the balance is ₹0 or a credit, so the 5.00 minimum does not apply.

Otherwise, the average is first rounded to one decimal place, with halves rounded up (so 4.45 counts as 4.5), and that rounded value is compared to the cut-offs: "Excellent" if it is 4.45 or higher, "Good" if it is 3.45 or higher but below 4.45, "Fair" if it is 2.45 or higher but below 3.45, and "Poor" if it is below 2.45. A parcel's charge is the zone's starting charge (₹9 for zone 2) for the first 500 g, plus ₹1 for each further 500 g block started beyond the first 500 g, so the number of blocks is the weight in grams divided by 500, rounded up, and the charge is starting charge + (blocks − 1) × ₹1; for example 2.5 kg is 5 blocks and costs ₹9 + 4 × ₹1 = ₹13, 2.501 kg is 6 blocks and costs ₹14, and a parcel of 0 g is charged nothing (₹0). A parcel over 20 kg also gets a flat ₹25 added on top of that charge, and the total never goes above ₹99.00.

The shipping calculator accepts every weight with no refusal and no weight limit: a parcel weighing 0 g or less is charged ₹0.00, and any heavier parcel (including a 120 kg pallet) is charged by weight as usual, except that the charge is capped at ₹99.00 in every zone.

Shipping is always charged and is determined only by the parcel's weight and zone, never by order value, and there is no free-shipping threshold, so a 2 kg parcel is charged the standard rate for 2 kg in its zone even when the basket is worth ₹2,500.

Compute the score as the number of promoters (answers of 9 or 10) minus the number of detractors (answers of 0 to 6), divided by the total number of valid answers (which includes the 7s and 8s), times 100, rounded to a whole number; ignore blank, non-numeric and outside-0-to-10 answers entirely, and show no score when there are fewer than 5 valid answers.

When computing the survey score, skip any blank answer and any score of 11 (excluding them from the total), but count a 7.5 as a valid answer included in the total that is neither a promoter nor a detractor, without capping or rounding any value and without rejecting the survey.

  Rule 7: Whenever age_years is given a date followed by a time after a space or a 'T' (for example 2000-01-01 10:00:00), it ignores everything after the date; spaces before or after the date are also ignored, but any other trailing characters directly after the date make it return NULL.
  What should it be? > A date followed by a time is not accepted: if there is anything after the date other than spaces or line breaks, including a time after a space or a "T", the result is NULL. Spaces or line breaks before or after the date alone are ignored.
  Rule 9: Whenever due_date is given an invoice date and a number of days, it returns the invoice date plus that many calendar days as YYYY-MM-DD, carrying over month ends and leap days (31 Jan 2024 + 30 days gives 2024-03-01; 28 Feb 2023 + 1 day gives 2023-03-01).
  What should it be? > If the due date lands on a Saturday or Sunday, it moves forward to the next Monday. The number of days added is also capped between 0 and 365: negative terms count as 0, and anything over 365 counts as 365.
  Rule 10: Whenever due_date is given 0 days, it returns the invoice date itself; whenever it is given a negative number of days, it returns an earlier date by that many days.
  What should it be? > With 0 days or negative days, the due date is the invoice date itself, because negative terms count as 0 and never move the date earlier. If that date is a Saturday or Sunday, it still moves forward to the next Monday.
  Rule 11: Whenever due_date is given days with a fractional part, it drops the fraction towards zero before adding (2.9 days counts as 2, -2.9 days counts as -2).
  What should it be? > Days with a fractional part are rounded down to the whole day before the 0–365 cap applies, so 2.9 days counts as 2. Negative fractions also round down, but they then count as 0 because negative terms never move the date earlier.
  Rule 12: Whenever due_date is given the days as text that is entirely a number (for example '30', ' 10 ', '2.9' or '1e2'), it uses that number; text that is not entirely a number ('abc', '', '12days') makes it return NULL, and text with underscores between digits ('1_0') is read as 10.
  What should it be? > Days given as text, even numeric text like '30' or '2.9', make due_date return NULL, and so does an empty text or any other non-number text. Only a real number is accepted for the days. A true/false value or binary data for the days also returns NULL, not 1 day.
  Rule 13: Whenever due_date is given a true value for the days it treats it as 1 day, and whenever it is given binary data for the days it returns NULL.
  What should it be? > A true/false value for the days makes due_date return NULL, not 1 day. Binary data for the days also returns NULL.
  Rule 16: Whenever due_date is given an invoice date followed by a time after a space or a 'T', it ignores the time and returns only the due date without a time.
  What should it be? > An invoice date followed by a time, whether after a space or a "T", is not accepted and the due date is NULL. Only spaces or line breaks before or after the date are ignored.
  Rule 17: Whenever due_date would produce a date beyond 9999-12-31 (or before year 1), or is given an absurdly large number of days, it returns NULL.
  What should it be? > There is no special rule for this. Days over 365 count as 365, so a huge number of days is not an error. Infinite or non-numeric days give NULL. Only an invoice date within the last year before 9999-12-31 can push the due date past 9999-12-31. My policy does not define a result for that case.
  Rule 22: Whenever initials is given an empty text or text made only of spaces, it returns an empty text, and whenever it is given NULL it returns NULL.
  What should it be? > Empty text, text made only of spaces, and NULL all give NULL. There is no initial to show, so the result is NULL rather than an empty text.
  Rule 24: Whenever invoice_check_digit is given a code made only of the digits 0-9, it returns a single digit from 0 to 9 using the standard retail (GS1) weighting: starting from the rightmost digit, digits are weighted 3, 1, 3, 1 and so on, summed, and the result is whatever brings the sum up to the next multiple of 10 (4006381333931 gives 4 and 400638133393 gives 1).
  What should it be? > Only the last 12 digits of the code count, and any digits before them are ignored. Those 12 are weighted 3, 1, 3, 1 and so on, starting from the rightmost one. The check digit is whatever brings the sum up to the next multiple of 10. So 4006381333931 gives 6, not 4, and 400638133393 still gives 1.
  Rule 27: Whenever invoice_check_digit is given a code with spaces or line breaks before or after it, it ignores them; spaces or hyphens inside the code, letters, a minus sign, a decimal point, or non-Western digits make it return NULL.
  What should it be? > Spaces, hyphens, letters, a minus sign, a decimal point and non-Western digits inside the code are not errors. Every character that is not a digit 0-9 is simply thrown away before the check digit is worked out, so '123-45', '12a' and '1.5' still give a digit. Only a code with no digits left at all (empty, only spaces or only letters) gives NULL.
  Rule 30: Whenever late_fee is given a positive balance in cents and a number of days late from 1 to 30, it charges 2% of the balance; for 31 to 60 days late it charges 4%; for 61 days or more it charges 6%.
  What should it be? > The fee is 2% of the balance for each 30-day period late, with a part period counted as a full one. So 6 to 30 days late is 2%, 31 to 60 days is 4%, 61 to 90 days is 6%, and so on. It keeps growing, with no stop at 6%. Up to 5 days late, nothing is charged. The fee is never below 500 cents and never above 5000 cents. Any fraction of a cent is rounded up.
  Rule 31: Whenever late_fee is given a number of days late that falls between whole days, it compares it exactly with the limits: 30.5 days is treated as more than 30 and so is charged 4%, and 60.5 days is charged 6%; any positive fraction of a day such as 0.5 counts as late and is charged 2%.
  What should it be? > Fractions of a day are compared exactly. Anything up to and including 5 days late is not charged, so 0.5 days late is 0. Anything over 5 days, such as 5.5, is charged 2% (a part period counts as a full one). Anything over 30 days, such as 30.5, is charged 4%, and anything over 60 days is charged 6%, and so on for each further 30 days.
  Rule 32: Whenever late_fee calculates a fee that is not a whole number of cents, it rounds to the nearest cent with exactly half a cent rounded up (a 125 cent balance at 2% gives 3, 75 gives 2, 24 gives 0, 25 gives 1).
  What should it be? > Any fraction of a cent is rounded up to the next whole cent, not to the nearest. For example, 25,001 cents at 2% is 500.02 cents, and that is charged as 501. After that rounding, the fee is raised to 500 cents if it is below that and capped at 5000 cents if it is above.
  Rule 33: Whenever late_fee is given zero or negative days late (not yet overdue), or a zero or negative balance, it returns 0 and charges nothing.
  What should it be? > A zero or negative balance, or zero or negative days late, charges nothing (0). The 500-cent minimum fee does not apply in that case, and neither does the 5-day grace rule.
  Rule 35: Whenever late_fee is given a balance or days late as text, it reads the number at the start of the text (' 500 ' is 500, '10000' is 10000), and text with no number at the start ('abc' or an empty text) is treated as 0 and so gives a fee of 0.
  What should it be? > Text for the balance or the days late, even numeric text such as '500' or '10', makes late_fee return NULL, and so does an empty or non-number text. Only real numbers are accepted.
  Rule 36: Whenever late_fee is given a balance with a fractional cent (10000.5), it applies the percentage to the exact value and rounds the fee as normal.
  What should it be? > A balance with a fractional cent (such as 10000.5) is accepted as a real number. The percentage is applied to the exact value, any fraction of a cent in the fee is rounded up, and then the 500-cent minimum and 5000-cent maximum apply. For example, 100000.5 cents at 10 days late gives 2001 rather than 2000.
  Rule 40: Whenever mask_card is given characters other than spaces and hyphens, such as letters, dots or tabs, it treats them like digits: they are counted, masked and may appear in the last four ('4111.1111' gives '*****1111').
  What should it be? > Every character that is not a digit 0-9 is thrown away before masking, so dots, letters and tabs are not counted or shown. When fewer than 12 digits are left, the result is one asterisk per remaining digit, and no digit is shown. So '4111.1111' gives '********', and 'ab12' gives '**'. With 12 or more digits, every digit except the last four becomes an asterisk.
  Rule 43: Whenever normalize_sku is given a SKU, it removes leading and trailing spaces, turns every run of spaces, tabs, line breaks and hyphens (in any mix) into one single hyphen, and changes the English letters a-z to capitals ('  abc   --  123  ' gives 'ABC-123').
  What should it be? > Leading and trailing spaces are removed, and each run of spaces, tabs or line breaks becomes a single hyphen. Hyphens already in the SKU are kept as they are and are not merged, so '  abc   --  123  ' gives 'ABC----123'. All letters are made capital. Any character that is not a letter or digit (apart from hyphens) is thrown away, so 'a_b' gives 'AB'. If nothing is left, the result is NULL.
  Rule 44: Whenever normalize_sku is given a SKU that starts or ends with hyphens, the hyphens are removed ('-abc-' gives 'ABC'), and a SKU made only of hyphens, only of spaces or empty returns an empty text.
  What should it be? > Hyphens at the start or end of a SKU are kept, not removed ('-abc-' gives '-ABC-'), and a SKU made only of hyphens keeps them ('---' gives '---'). A SKU that is empty or only spaces gives NULL.
  Rule 45: Whenever normalize_sku is given letters with accents or from other alphabets, it leaves them unchanged, only the plain English letters a-z become capitals ('élan-ß' gives 'éLAN-ß').
  What should it be? > Accented letters and letters from other alphabets are thrown away, so 'élan-ß' gives 'LAN-SS'. The one exception is ß, which becomes 'SS' and is kept.
  Rule 46: Whenever normalize_sku is given other separators such as underscores, slashes, dots or a longer dash (–), it keeps them unchanged.
  What should it be? > Underscores, slashes, dots and longer dashes are not kept. They are thrown away, so 'a_b' gives 'AB' and 'a.b' gives 'AB'. Only letters, digits and hyphens survive, and spaces, tabs and line breaks turn into hyphens.
  Rule 49: Whenever rating_label is given an average score of 4.5 to 5 and at least one review, it returns 'Excellent'; for 3.5 up to but not including 4.5 it returns 'Good'; for 2.5 up to but not including 3.5 it returns 'Average'; below 2.5 (down to 0) it returns 'Poor'.
  What should it be? > The score is first rounded to one decimal place, with halves rounded up. A rounded score of 4.5 or more is 'Excellent', so 4.45 counts as Excellent. 3.5 up to 4.5 is 'Good', 2.5 up to 3.5 is 'Fair' (not 'Average'), and anything lower is 'Poor'. These labels only apply when there are at least 5 reviews. With fewer than 5 reviews the label is 'Unrated', even with a perfect score.
  Rule 50: Whenever rating_label is given a review count of zero or less and a valid average score, it returns 'No reviews' whatever the score is (a score of 0 with no reviews gives 'No reviews', not 'Poor').
  What should it be? > With zero or fewer reviews the label is "Unrated", whatever the score is, so a score of 0 with no reviews also gives "Unrated", not "No reviews". The label is also "Unrated" for any count under 5, such as 0.5 reviews.
  Rule 51: Whenever rating_label is given a review count between 0 and 1 (such as 0.5), it counts as having reviews and uses the score bands.
  What should it be? > A review count between 0 and 1, such as 0.5, does not count as having reviews. Any count under 5 gives "Unrated", whatever the score.
  Rule 52: Whenever rating_label is given an average score below 0 or above 5, it returns NULL, even when the review count is zero.
  What should it be? > A score below 0 or above 5 gives the label "Invalid", whatever the review count is, including zero reviews.
  Rule 55: Whenever shipping_cost is given a weight in grams and a delivery zone of 1, 2 or 3, it returns a base charge in cents of 500 for zone 1, 700 for zone 2 and 900 for zone 3, plus 200 cents for each started kilogram (1 gram to 1000 grams is one kilogram, 1001 grams is two).
  What should it be? > Base charge is 500 cents for zone 1, 800 for zone 2 and 1200 for zone 3. On top of that, each started 500 grams adds 100 cents (1 to 500 grams is one step, 501 grams is two). A zone other than 1, 2 or 3 (such as 4, 0 or 1.5) is not rejected; it is charged like zone 3.
  Rule 56: Whenever shipping_cost is given a weight with a fraction of a gram (such as 0.5 or 1000.5), it still charges every started kilogram, so 0.5 grams counts as one kilogram and 1000.5 grams as two.
  What should it be? > A fraction of a gram still counts as a started 500 grams, so 0.5 grams is one step (100 cents), 500.5 grams is two steps, and 1000.5 grams is three steps.
  Rule 57: Whenever shipping_cost is given a weight of zero or less, it returns NULL (no charge is given).
  What should it be? > A weight of zero or less is not charged at all: the shipping cost is 0, not NULL, and the base charge does not apply either.
  Rule 58: Whenever shipping_cost is given a zone other than 1, 2 or 3 (such as 0, 4, a negative number or 1.5), it returns NULL; a zone written as 2.0 is accepted as zone 2.
  What should it be? > A zone other than 1, 2 or 3 (such as 0, 4, a negative number or 1.5) is not rejected: it is charged exactly like zone 3. A zone written as 2.0 is accepted as zone 2.
  Rule 61: Whenever shipping_cost is given a very heavy weight it keeps adding 200 cents per started kilogram without any cap or upper limit (100000 grams in zone 3 gives 20900).
  What should it be? > Heavy parcels are capped. Any parcel over 20 kilograms (20,000 grams) gets a surcharge of 2,500 cents on top of the normal charge. The total shipping charge never goes above 9,900 cents, so 100,000 grams in zone 3 gives 9,900, not 20,900.
  Rule 67: Whenever nps_score has no valid response at all (an empty column, only NULLs, only out-of-range values or only text), it returns NULL.
  What should it be? > It returns NULL whenever there are fewer than 5 valid responses, not only when there are none. Responses that are NULL, below 0, above 10 or text are ignored and don't count. So with 4 valid responses, or with 0, the result is NULL.
  Rule 68: Whenever nps_score is used with groups or a filter, it works out the score separately for the rows in each group or the rows that pass the filter; asking for DISTINCT scores makes no difference, as duplicates are still counted.
  What should it be? > DISTINCT does change the result: only each different score is counted once, so duplicate responses are not counted. Groups and filters are right: the score is worked out separately for each group or for the rows that pass the filter. The 5-valid-response minimum applies to each group or filtered set on its own, and a group with fewer than 5 valid responses gives NULL.
  Anything the builders should know that is not on this list? (Enter = nothing) > Initials skip the lowercase name particles (van, von, de, da, di, la, del, der, den, du, le) but not capitalised ones, so "Vincent van Gogh" gives VG while "Jean Van Damme" gives JVD. Each space-separated word gives one initial, so "Mary-Jane Smith" gives MS, and a name with no initials left gives NULL. A person is NULL years old if the as-of date is before the birth date or if either date is not a valid YYYY-MM-DD date. A card number or code given as a whole number is accepted as if it were text, so 4111111111111111 is masked like the text version and 4006381333 gets a check digit.
